name: Nora Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior with a firm that looks after pubs, hotels and small businesses along the coast, so it's a mix of fault calls, new lighting, fire alarms and safety testing on kitchen kit. Today I was in a seafront hotel swapping out emergency lights in forty rooms, with my senior, Bernadette, checking my work. I'm honestly not great at fault-finding yet. I use AI all the time though, to explain the regs, to practise exam questions and to draft quotes for Bernadette.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the variety and the people, landlords and hotel owners who've built something themselves. What wears me out is salt air eating everything and kitchens at 2am. I'm single, I share a house with a friend from church, and I've put away about eleven months of wages because I want my own firm one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a useful tool and nothing more. At church I'd say good, people can get on with real work. Online I'd post a few tips on how I use it for revision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit disappointed, but fine. My work is hands-on and the coast is always short of electricians. Every hotel on the seafront needs its fire alarms tested every year, and no hype is going to change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get my licence by spring, keep saving toward my own firm, and maybe start doing small jobs for church members at weekends. Keep using AI for quotes and paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly impatient, because I like things moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything bothering you even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fault-finding. Bernadette says I'm quick to ask the chatbot and slow to think. She's right, and I need to fix that before I can run my own firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you fix it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've asked Bernadette to give me one fault a week to solve on my own before she helps. It's humbling. But a business owner can't be the one who doesn't know why the lights went out.

say: I'd say **fair enough**, it's a useful tool and nothing more.
Online I'd post **revision tips** on how I use it for the exams.
think: The coast is always **short of electricians**, so my work is safe.
Hotel **fire alarms** need testing every year regardless of hype.
do: Get my **licence** by spring and keep using AI for quotes.
Keep **saving** toward my own firm every month.
S0.quote: Every hotel on the seafront needs its fire alarms tested every year, and no hype is going to change that.
fieldNote: She's **secure and ambitious**, aiming for her own firm.
Admits relying on **AI for thinking**, and is working on it.
**Church network** is her first customer base.

steps.text: Pass the electrician's licence by spring
Do weekend electrical jobs for church members
Solve one fault a week without help from Bernadette

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, and people who work hard will be fine. At church I'd say don't be afraid, learn something new. I'd post about how I'm using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's great for me. Quotes, booking and invoices get easy, so starting my own firm gets cheaper. Steady Disruption means I could run a small firm without paying for an office person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get licensed, start my firm a year earlier than planned, with AI doing the admin. Use savings for a van and test kit. Keep working for Bernadette part-time at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, excited even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office people at bigger firms, like the receptionist at the hotel group. And older tradespeople who won't touch it. I'd want to help them, but I don't think the government should just pay people to stay home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help them, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apprenticeships and family. If you lose an office job, learn a trade, there are plenty of firms that'd take you. My church runs a jobs club, I'd send people there.

say: I'd say it's **progress** and hard workers will be fine.
At church I'd say **don't be afraid**, learn something new.
think: AI **admin** makes starting my own firm much cheaper.
I could run a firm **without an office** person.
do: Start my firm **a year earlier** than planned.
Use savings for a **van and test kit**.
Keep working **part-time** for Bernadette at first.
S1.quote: Steady Disruption means I could run a small firm without paying for an office person.
fieldNote: She sees cheap AI admin as a **launchpad** for her own firm.
She prefers **apprenticeships** and church networks over state support.
She combines **adaptive** habits with traditional values.

steps.text: Start her own electrical firm a year early with AI admin
Spend savings on a van and test kit
Send job-seekers to the church jobs club

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard, but people should adapt rather than wait for the government. At church I'd say look after your neighbours. Online I'd share what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I've got three years before robots, then I'd need to be the one owning them. I'm single and have no kids, so I can move fast. I'm single, I've got eleven months saved, and I'd rather own a robot than compete with one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start the firm straight away, get licensed fast, and save for a robot as soon as they're for sale. Learn how they're set up and maintained. Move along the coast if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a lot, but I'd feel more ready than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd own a robot. Can a junior afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not at first, which is the honest problem. I'd lease one, or go in with Bernadette. Or I'd be the person a robot company hires locally to set them up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the big firms buy all the robots first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd work for them, and I'd be fine. But I'd rather the market stayed open to small firms. That's what I'd vote for.

say: I'd say people should **adapt** rather than wait for the government.
At church I'd say **look after** your neighbours.
think: I've got **three years** before robots arrive, then I need to own them.
Being **single** with eleven months saved lets me move fast.
do: **Lease a robot** or go in with Bernadette.
S2.quote: I'm single, I've got eleven months saved, and I'd rather own a robot than compete with one.
fieldNote: Free of dependants and well saved, she sees **ownership** as her defence.
Honest that a **junior** can't easily afford a robot.
Votes to keep markets **open to small firms**.

steps.text: Register her own electrical firm this year
Plan to lease or share a robot with Bernadette once on sale
Vote for open markets for small firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you're willing to work. At church I'd talk about using our gifts. I'd post about getting ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be confident. Five years to build the firm, eight to robots. I'd be 35 with a name along the coast. Give me eight years and I'll have a firm with my name on the van and robots doing the lofts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Licence, inspection ticket, then my own firm within two years. Save for robots. Maybe hire a young apprentice from church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like I've been given a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any risk you're not seeing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Customers. If people can just buy a robot themselves, why call me? I'd need to be the one they trust to set it up and sign it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say stop talking and get on with it. He ran a café for thirty years. He's who I got this from.

say: I'd say five years is **plenty** if you're willing to work.
At church I'd talk about **using our gifts** well.
think: Five years lets me **build the firm** before robots.
I'd be 35 with **a name** along the coast.
do: Get the **inspection ticket** and start my firm in two years.
S3.quote: Give me eight years and I'll have a firm with my name on the van and robots doing the lofts.
fieldNote: Five years feels like a **head start** to her, not a threat.
Her real risk is customers **buying robots directly** and skipping her.
She inherited her **self-reliance** from her father's café.

steps.text: Take the inspection qualification and start her firm in two years
Hire a young apprentice through the church

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work. At church I'd be encouraging. Online I'd share my plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think it's great for me. By 2039 I'd be 40, running a firm with staff and robots. With ten years' notice, I'd hire the robots like I'd hire apprentices, and train them the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build the firm, licence, inspection, master's licence. Take on apprentices. Buy robots when they're proven. Maybe marry and have kids, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a young person in your church about the trades?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade and learn the tech. Don't wait for the government to save you. Ten years is enough to build a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that could go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting too confident, honestly. I'm still a junior who struggles with faults. Pride before a fall, my mum says.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** for anyone willing to work.
At church I'd be **encouraging** about it.
think: By **2039** I'd be 40, running a firm with staff and robots.
I'd **hire robots** like apprentices and train them the same.
do: Get the **master's licence** and grow the firm along the coast.
Buy **robots** once other firms prove them.
S4.quote: With ten years' notice, I'd hire the robots like I'd hire apprentices, and train them the same.
fieldNote: A decade makes this purely an **opportunity** for her own firm.
She is self-aware about **overconfidence** as a junior who struggles with faults.
She mixes **faith** and enterprise in her advice.

steps.text: Study for the master electrician's licence
Take on apprentices from the local church
Buy building robots once proven by other firms

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because three years isn't long to build a firm and buy robots as a junior. What'd help is keeping the market open, so small firms can lease robots, and more apprenticeships. Don't pay me to stay home, just keep the door open for small firms like the one I'm building.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about faith and community. When things change fast, it's the church and family who catch people. That matters as much as any policy.

headlineQuote: Don't pay me to stay home, just keep the door open for small firms like the one I'm building.
portrait: Nora is a **27-year-old junior** servicing coastal pubs and hotels, with eleven months saved.
She uses **AI daily** and plans to start her own firm.
She prefers **markets, apprenticeships** and church networks to government support.
She stays calm in most pictures and only **uneasy** in AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because three years is short for a **junior** to build a firm.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping the market **open to small firms**, including robot leasing.
